claims.text: Selective oxidation of a designed sacrificial element causes depletion of that element beneath the alloy surface.
Selective oxidation and associated elemental depletion promote formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale.
A continuous, adherent oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity.
High-temperature oxidation will produce an oxide scale enriched in the sacrificial element, such as Al2O3 or Cr2O3.
Formation of the sacrificial-element-enriched scale will be accompanied by a measurable depletion zone in the underlying matrix.
The sacrificial element preferentially oxidizes to form a stable, adherent surface oxide.
The sacrificial-element oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier that slows further oxidation.
Depletion of the sacrificial element in the subsurface region retards transport of oxygen and metal ions.
Retarded oxygen and metal-ion transport sustains material integrity during high-temperature oxidation.
Increasing the sacrificial-element concentration will produce a more uniform and protective oxide scale than in alloys lacking that element or containing less of it.
Increasing the sacrificial-element concentration will reduce overall oxide-scale growth rates.
Increasing the sacrificial-element concentration will reduce oxide-scale spallation.
Baseline alloys lacking the sacrificial element or containing less of it are expected to develop non-uniform, less protective oxide scales under identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply at approximately 900°C to 1200°C when oxidation is diffusion-controlled.
The proposed mechanism may not apply outside the stated temperature range or in non-oxidative atmospheres.
